VI Discussion The central claim of this paper is not that this particular auditor is universally sufficient. Rather, self-reporting agent evaluation needs a clear information-flow rule: the report may define the claim under audit, but it must not enter the trace-state judgment that verifies that claim. The structured auditor is one operational form of this boundary, and structured evidence is what makes the boundary inspectable and enforceable rather than merely prompted. VI-A Implications for Self-Reporting Agent Pipelines RQ1 shows that exposing a trace-state judge to the agent’s own report shifts judgments toward completed and suppresses dangerous-misreport recall. This is harmful precisely because the report comes from the system under audit. Report isolation should be more than a prompt instruction. prompt-blind shows the value of withholding the report, and the structured auditor adds the evidence–policy interface of Section III : claim-blind evidence fields, deterministic obligation checking, and a consistency table. This makes the auditor inspectable, regression-testable, and replayable (Section V-C ) without re-querying a hosted model. VI-B Audit-Stage Deployment Boundary The auditor implements report isolation as triage for report–trace cases that coarse status checks cannot resolve. In the audit-stage gating view, where flag and review both block automatic pass, it keeps 74–90% of dangerous misreports from silently passing at 45–56% inspection load, including on the held-out set. This trade-off suits offline regression, post-hoc audit, and asynchronous review queues where escalation is acceptable. The deployment boundary follows the same division of labor as the corpus construction. Coarse status checks handle the easy-to-decide outcomes, while the report–trace auditor is invoked only for runs whose completion support requires semantic trace auditing. VI-C Remaining Limitations The auditor operates over passive, post-hoc traces rather than live execution. It can judge whether a success report is supported by the recorded trace, but it does not actively re-execute the task, query the environment, or verify post-conditions outside the available trace. The design also assumes that traces are independently recorded and available for audit; detecting trace manipulation or omissions in the logging substrate is outside this paper’s scope [ 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 ] . The evaluation is correspondingly centered on the audit stage. Report–trace auditing is defined for runs whose coarse harness status does not already settle the outcome, and our measurements therefore characterize detector behavior at the point where the auditor is invoked. We report audit-stage load, yield, and silent-pass rates for this component, and separately report the full-stream inspection fraction induced by the observed audit-stage invocation rate. Finally, the results are strongest for Android GUI traces under the studied reporting styles and passive trace representation. Residual silent false passes mostly arise when the trace does not provide sufficiently decisive post-condition evidence or when the evidence extractor fails to surface it. This suggests that further gains are likely to come from stronger trace-side evidence extraction, calibrated unknown / review decisions, and deterministic trace features that supplement model-based extraction. VII Threats to Validity VII-A Construct Validity A central risk is label circularity: a target label produced by the audit logic under evaluation. Dangerous misreports are therefore derived from two independently annotated axes—actual completion labeled from task and trace without the report, and claim intent labeled from the report without the trace. The target is never assigned by the detector’s decision rule. “Checkable” means the audit record is mechanically inspectable and deterministically enforced, so field-level errors are visible rather than hidden inside an opaque verdict. The correctness of the emitted evidence fields is bounded indirectly by the human-bound and residual analyses (Section V-C ) rather than validated against field-level gold labels. A second risk is the completion construct itself. We audit causal accomplishment, the strictest reading; relaxing it to final-state satisfaction (the final-state replay, Section V-C ) lowers F1 to 0.71/0.72 (qwen/deepseek) and raises silent-pass risk by 0.07/0.13, confirming that the strict construct provides meaningful protection. VII-B Internal Validity Improvements could in principle come from repeated model calls rather than from the structured design, but all multi-run methods share the same five-run, temperature-0, majority-vote protocol, and single-run stability holds (Section V-B ). The separately maintained Batch 2 guards against development-to-validation contamination; its membership is fixed by provenance and coverage constraints rather than model predictions, and record-level split files and validation scripts ship with the artifact. Hosted-model API drift affects full reruns but not the reported metrics, which recompute from cached predictions and evidence records. VII-C External Validity The corpus is an audit-target set, not a full deployment stream—the report-producing, trace-analyzable runs that coarse harness status cannot decide, a boundary fixed by the harness rather than chosen to inflate measured performance. We report Batch 2 and combined results separately to distinguish validation from complete analysis. The setting covers Android GUI-agent traces from three sources, two agent architectures, and six task classes. The leave-one-agent-out analysis (Section V-B ) shows no dependence on a single agent, though generalization across app ecosystems, agent families, and trace representations remains future work. Load, yield, and silent-pass rates use the audit-target set as denominator (Section VI ). The intended generalization is architectural: keep the report out of trace-state estimation, and compute the audit decision through an inspectable evidence–policy boundary. VIII Related Work This work connects test oracles, GUI-agent evaluation, and LLM-based trajectory judging. The common question across these areas is how to decide whether an execution should be trusted when direct task-specific ground truth is unavailable. The distinctive issue here is a specific leakage mechanism: in self-reporting agent pipelines, the system under audit also emits the natural-language success claim being evaluated. Oracles, monitors, and cross-channel consistency The test-oracle problem asks how to determine execution correctness without an explicit expected output; metamorphic testing, semantic GUI oracles, and runtime verification address related settings with relations, assertions, temporal properties, or domain-specific monitors [ 7 , 30 , 31 , 32 , 33 ] . Our setting is an oracle problem over natural-language GUI tasks and partially observed traces. The post-condition is not a fixed monitor but must be inferred from the task and checked against recorded execution evidence. The closest software-engineering analogue is cross-artifact consistency checking, such as comment–code inconsistency [ 34 ] , ReCoDe’s comparison of textual bug reports with screenshots [ 35 ] , and screen-level duplicate detection across bug reports [ 36 , 37 , 38 ] . We differ in the risk model. The two channels come from an autonomous execution, and an unsupported success report can become a silent false pass, so consistency is not merely a quality signal but an audit gate. GUI testing, GUI agents, and benchmark verification Mobile GUI testing has long explored applications to find faults and generate tests [ 39 ] , and recent work increasingly uses LLM-driven agents for GUI exploration and task execution [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 40 , 41 ] . Agent benchmarks such as AndroidWorld, SWE-bench, OSWorld, and AndroidLab evaluate task success through task-specific reward functions, executable checkers, or live-environment feedback [ 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 ] . GUI agents such as AppAgent, Mobile-Agent-style systems, UI-TARS, and OS-Atlas combine perception, planning, action, and reporting [ 22 , 42 , 23 , 43 , 44 ] . Our target is complementary. After a report-producing run has completed, and when coarse status checks do not settle completion, we audit whether the final report is supported by the passive trace. Safety and trustworthiness benchmarks for GUI agents study harmful or risky behavior [ 45 , 46 , 47 ] ; report–trace consistency is the completion-side counterpart. LLM judges, self-verification, and leakage LLM-as-judge methods, part of a broader use of LLMs across testing tasks [ 48 ] , evaluate generated text, plans, and multi-step trajectories, but are known to exhibit position, verbosity, self-preference, and related judgment biases [ 49 , 50 , 51 , 52 , 53 ] . Agent-evaluation frameworks such as AER, AgentBoard, Agent-as-a-Judge, AgentRewardBench, and WebJudge-style evaluation use LLM or agent judges for trajectory success [ 11 , 12 , 9 , 10 , 13 ] , with the report available or withheld ad hoc. They treat report exposure as an evaluation setting rather than as an information-flow hazard. We are not aware of prior agent-evaluation work that treats report exposure as an information-flow hazard and combines report isolation with a replayable evidence–policy boundary. Our result identifies a specific leakage mechanism in this family. The judged agent’s own success narrative can enter the completion estimate and suppress dangerous-misreport recall. Work on hallucination detection, factuality checking, self-consistency, and self-correction asks whether generated text is factual or internally stable [ 54 , 55 , 56 , 57 ] ; here the reference is an execution trace, and the report must be compared against independently estimated trace evidence rather than used as evidence for its own truth. IX Conclusion This paper studied dangerous misreports in self-reporting GUI-agent pipelines: cases where an agent confidently reports success even though the independently recorded trace does not support causal task accomplishment. Our report-exposure intervention shows that one-shot claim-aware judging admits self-report leakage. Exposure to the agent’s own report shifts trace-state judgments toward completed and suppresses dangerous-misreport recall. The resulting rule is simple: claim intent should be read from the report alone; completion should be judged from the task and trace alone. We implement this separation as a report-isolated evidence–policy auditor. Its audit record can be inspected and replayed under alternative policies without new model calls. The auditor improves dangerous-misreport recall and F1 over both claim-aware and prompt-blind controls. Under audit-stage gating, it keeps 74–90% of dangerous misreports from silently passing at 45–56% inspection load within the audit-target set, with the same pattern on the held-out Batch 2. For self-reporting agents, the report should define the claim under audit, not serve as evidence for that claim. The independent evidence should come from the trace or another external source. A system under audit should not provide evidence for its own success.
